name: Root binding / container-restriction stress
summary: Container restriction is documented in hemp transplants, but canopy stress is nonspecific and roots touching a pot are not sufficient evidence. A defensible label requires plant-linked views of the intact root ball, repeatable boundary-following deformation or dense matting, and exclusion of dry-center irrigation failure, salinity, hypoxia, transplant injury, nematodes, and root disease.
affectedParts: crown and lower stem for exclusions
indicators: Multiple roots follow the container wall or bottom in repeated arcs, coils, or a dense boundary mat rather than extending radially through available substrate.
The extracted intact root mass retains the container geometry and shows a tight root-dominant perimeter across more than one face; one exposed root or a cohesive nursery root ball is insufficient.

The root-ball center and perimeter differ visibly in moisture after a documented irrigation event, consistent with preferential flow or incomplete wetting; this supports a water-delivery mechanism but is not specific to root binding.
A plant-linked whole-canopy comparison may show reduced expansion or vigor relative to a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-zone control, but canopy appearance is secondary evidence only.
In field-transplanted hemp, the original root architecture may remain constrained after transplant and poor establishment can coexist with secondary Fusarium or Pythium infection.

Time-matched root views show increasing wall-following deflection or matting before any post-transplant establishment failure, preserving the temporal link between container occupancy and later stress.
After transplant, serial plant-linked views show whether new roots cross the former container boundary; persistent confinement supports the survey observation but is not a universal prognosis.

Reduced growth is concordant with verified restricted rooting volume and intact-root morphology rather than inferred from container dimensions alone; the non-Cannabis meta-analysis supports growth effects but not a Cannabis diagnostic threshold.
exclusions: Do not label a plant from canopy stunting, wilt, chlorosis, marginal browning, or reduced vigor without a plant-linked intact root-ball inspection.
Do not treat a small container, roots visible at drainage holes, one perimeter root, or normal root-ball cohesion as proof of pathological restriction.
Exclude drought or irrigation channeling with measured center-versus-edge moisture before and after irrigation and a documented wetting pattern.
Exclude salinity or fertilizer concentration with calibrated root-zone EC and input/runoff records.
Exclude overwatering or hypoxia with moisture history, aeration context, odor, root color, and tissue integrity rather than inferring it from wilt alone.
Escalate brown, water-soaked, sloughed, necrotic, lesioned, or foul-smelling roots for culture or molecular testing for Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, and other root pathogens.
Inspect washed roots for discrete galls or abnormal swellings and obtain nematode confirmation when root-knot nematodes remain plausible.
Exclude transplant shock, torn roots, compressed plugs, buried crowns, stem girdling, and container heat injury using handling history and crown/root inspection.
Exclude detached, washed, cut, or cropped root images that lack a persistent plant and root-specimen identifier linking the intact root ball, container history, canopy, sampling event, and follow-up.

Do not use the non-Cannabis 43% mean biomass response, container volume, root density, number of circling roots, transplant timing, or post-transplant outcome as a universal Cannabis diagnostic threshold, severity rule, or production target.
After up-potting, prolonged wetness or decline is attributed to residual binding without checking excess wet medium, drainage, hypoxia, root damage and root disease in the new container.

progression.description: Root tips reach a physical boundary; contact or an occasional deflected root is normal and not diagnostic.
Repeated roots begin following the wall or bottom; record the number of affected faces and preserve an intact comparison root ball.
Wall-following roots become a tight root-dominant layer and may alter wetting, but moisture and EC measurements are still required to identify the stress mechanism.
Cannabis-specific survey evidence reports that some root-bound hemp transplants did not reliably overcome the bound architecture after field transplanting.

UGA ornamental guidance warns that an oversized replacement pot can retain moisture longer and increase root-disease risk. Treat this as a separate water/root-health differential, not proof of persistent Cannabis root binding.
Poor establishment may overlap Fusarium or Pythium; later discoloration or decay must not be attributed to mechanical restriction alone.

lookAlikes: Normal cohesive nursery root ball or vigorous roots at drainage holes
Irrigation channeling or hydrophobic substrate without mechanical root restriction
Transplant shock or mechanical root tearing
Stem girdling, buried crown, or compressed propagation plug
Field soil compaction or a tillage pan restricting rooting depth
Nutrient deficiency caused by pH or root-zone chemistry
confirmation: Before disturbing roots, record a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy, container size and shape, substrate surface, drainage openings, crown, and all accessible root-ball faces with a metric scale and neutral color reference.

Extract the root ball intact and photograph the top, bottom, and at least four side quadrants; then gently remove substrate and repeat the views so normal cohesion can be separated from repeated container-contour roots.
Capture a matched same-cultivar, same-age, same-substrate, same-irrigation comparison plant using identical views and exposure; do not infer restriction from an unmatched small-pot image.
Measure root-zone moisture at the center and perimeter immediately before and after a documented irrigation event, and record input and leachate EC plus pH with calibrated instruments.
Document root color, firmness, odor, lesions, sloughing, crown integrity, and discrete galls; submit representative plant-linked tissue for pathogen or nematode testing when those signs are present.

For a post-transplant sequence, keep plant identity linked across dates and include the original root-ball boundary plus new roots beyond it; do not use canopy recovery or failure alone as confirmation.

Keep canopy-only, detached-root-only, non-Cannabis transfer, unmatched, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear samples out of the confirmed class and all automated training splits.

Assign persistent plant and root-specimen identifiers before disturbance and carry them through intact and washed root views, container and transplant history, moisture and chemistry measurements, laboratory results, canopy images, and follow-up observations.

Keep compatible root-ball morphology, verified restricted rooting volume, irrigation nonuniformity, salinity, hypoxia, infectious or nematode findings, post-transplant persistence, and causally attributed container-restriction injury as separate labels.

For post-repotting decline, pair dated root views with old/new container dimensions, drainage and center/perimeter wetting records. Firm, pale roots are inspection context, not a laboratory-negative pathogen result; retain disease testing when indicated.

For field transplants, pair the former plug boundary with a scaled surrounding soil-profile view and cultivation-depth history. Record whether roots remain in the old plug or encounter a deeper compacted layer; separate these observations from canopy drought and test moisture and root-health alternatives independently.

For quantitative root-distribution records, retain species, container geometry, image modality, region definitions, resolution and segmentation masks; distinguish volumetric measurements from surface-only root-ball photographs and do not impute unseen fine roots.
immediateActions: Preserve and document at least one intact symptomatic root ball and one matched comparison before cutting, teasing, washing, transplanting, or changing irrigation.
Measure center/perimeter moisture, EC, pH, and drainage behavior while screening for root decay and galls; avoid assigning the cause from pot size or canopy appearance.
Quarantine or segregate plants with root lesions, decay, or galls until infectious and nematode differentials are evaluated.
correctivePlan: Use crop-stage- and production-system-appropriate transplant or root-management practices only after physical restriction is confirmed; the non-Cannabis sources do not validate a universal Cannabis root-pruning method.
Correct verified irrigation nonuniformity, salinity, hypoxia, or infection as separate coexisting problems rather than assuming that relieving container restriction resolves them.

Track new roots beyond the former container boundary and compare canopy development with matched controls; retain the record as uncertain if root expansion and plant response are not temporally linked.
prevention: Match container volume and transplant timing to cultivar growth rate and production duration, and audit representative intact root balls before transplant batches are moved.
Record container history, up-pot dates, irrigation delivery, substrate, cultivar, and plant age so boundary deformation can be interpreted against an appropriate comparison.
Reject or flag incoming transplants with severe repeated circling/matting, decay, galls, or an undocumented root-zone history for human review.
warnings: Photo or video alone cannot establish the physiological cause of canopy stress; root-ball morphology, plant linkage, measurements, and exclusion checks are required.

The controlled rooting-volume meta-analysis and University of Maryland morphology guide are non-Cannabis transfer evidence and do not establish Cannabis thresholds, universal symptoms, severity, or treatment efficacy.

The hemp evidence is a diagnostic survey rather than a controlled container-size trial, so cultivar response, incidence, timing, yield effect, and a pathological root-density threshold remain unresolved.
Root binding can coexist with Fusarium, Pythium, irrigation failure, or salinity; finding circling roots does not exclude a more proximate cause of decline.

UGA repotting guidance is non-Cannabis ornamental transfer context: do not turn its pot-size increment, seasonal timing or pruning advice into a Cannabis prescription. Post-repotting wetness and root appearance require independent confirmation and human review when causality remains unresolved.

One institutional non-Cannabis pot-bound root-mass photograph is indexed as copyright-restricted reference metadata only; no licensed, plant-linked Cannabis root-binding progression image or verified diagnostic video was located.

A second institutional reference shows hemp roots, but remains rights-unclear metadata only. The OSU catalog currently associates its rootbound-hemp caption with a wheat-field asset; use the separately inspected UC Davis Figure 2 root photograph, not that mismatched asset. Neither is confirmed causal ground truth.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

sources.title: Pot size matters: a meta-analysis of the effects of rooting volume on plant growth
supportedClaims: A meta-analysis of 65 plant studies found that doubling pot size increased biomass by 43% on average and that reduced growth in smaller pots was associated mainly with lower photosynthesis per unit leaf area.

The analysis establishes that rooting volume can materially alter plant growth, but it is not Cannabis-specific and does not validate a universal Cannabis container size, root-density threshold, visual symptom, or field diagnosis.

The authors caution that appropriate pot size depends on plant size; the paper's experimental biomass-per-volume proposal is research-design guidance and is not a diagnostic threshold for cultivated Cannabis.

MRI observations in barley and sugar beet placed 20–25% of root biomass in the inner half of the soil volume and roughly half within the outer 4 mm. Dataset inference: these non-Cannabis regional fractions are not Cannabis diagnostic thresholds or percentages assignable from a surface photograph.

The MRI analysis thresholded images, excluded the stem and developing storage beet, and integrated pixel values by soil region; the finest roots could go undetected. Dataset inference: retain modality and segmentation limits with root-distribution measurements, rather than treating visible root area or counts in photographs as equivalent measurements.

sources.title: Pot-Bound Indoor Plants
sources.organization: University of Maryland Extension, Home & Garden Information Center
authors: University of Maryland Extension Home & Garden Information Center
supportedClaims: The institutional guide describes pot-bound morphology in non-Cannabis indoor plants as roots encircling the pot perimeter and forming a tight mass that can fill the pot or extend over its edge.
It also reports that water can pass through a pot-bound root mass too quickly while the root-ball center remains dry, and that resulting desiccation can produce tip dieback or marginal browning.

These morphology and watering observations are transfer context only: they support root-ball inspection and drought exclusion but do not establish Cannabis ground truth, severity, progression, or a camera-only diagnosis.

The page labels an institutional photograph as a pot-bound plant and shows an extracted non-Cannabis root mass beside its container; it is morphology-planning context only and does not establish a Cannabis diagnosis, plant linkage, progression, or causal stress.

sources.title: Repotting Container Plants for Long-Term Health
supportedClaims: The guide concerns ornamental trees, shrubs and flowering perennials, not a Cannabis container-size experiment; its 3–4-inch pot-diameter increment and seasonal repotting advice are not Cannabis treatment standards.
An unnecessarily large replacement container can leave excess medium wet longer and increase root-disease risk; adequate drainage and root inspection remain necessary after repotting.

The guide describes firm, light-colored healthy roots and inspection for damaged or decayed roots. Using that appearance as inspection context rather than proof of pathogen absence is a dataset annotation safeguard, not a validated exclusion test.

sources.title: Planning a drought-resilient hemp crop
supportedClaims: EM 9628, published July 2022 and reviewed in 2026, identifies both root binding and soil compaction as limits to accessible soil volume in hemp; restricted moisture access is not specific to container binding.

The guide distinguishes greenhouse-origin root binding with possible season-long effects from a tillage pan below cultivated soil. Dataset inference: field capture should pair the former plug boundary with the surrounding soil profile rather than diagnose either mechanism from canopy drought symptoms.

Its single root close-up is an institutional morphology reference, not a paired disease exclusion, moisture assay, time series, or confirmed causal injury sample; no item-level reuse permission is stated.
